notes.meaning: Daniel receives a second vision about two years after his first one in chapter 7. Babylon was still ruled by King Belshazzar, but its empire was nearing its end. Here the book switches back to Hebrew, showing that the message directly concerns God's covenant people.

In the vision, Daniel sees himself transported to the citadel of Susa beside the Ulai canal. Susa was an important city in Elam that would later become a chief capital of the Persian Empire. God showed him this place because the events in the vision would soon happen there.

Daniel looks up and sees a ram with two long horns standing by the canal. The two horns stand for the joint empire of the Medes and the Persians. The horn that grew up later and became taller represents Persia, which started smaller but soon became much stronger than Media.

The ram charges west, north, and south, conquering lands in every direction. No other nation can stop it or rescue anyone from its power. It does whatever it wants and grows very proud in its greatness.

Suddenly a male goat charges from the west across the whole earth so quickly that its feet do not even seem to touch the ground. This goat represents Greece, and the large horn between its eyes represents its first great conqueror, Alexander the Great. Alexander marched across the ancient world with astonishing speed.

The goat rushes at the two-horned ram in violent anger and shatters both of its horns. The ram has no strength to resist, so the goat knocks it down, tramples it, and leaves no one to save it. This pictures the fierce Greek victories that crushed the Persian army and overthrew the entire Persian Empire.

The goat becomes extremely powerful, but at the very height of its strength, its large horn snaps off. In its place, four noticeable horns grow up pointing toward the four winds. This foretells Alexander dying suddenly in his youth, after which his empire was divided among four of his leading generals.

Out of one of those four horns comes a little horn that starts small but grows very powerful toward the south, the east, and the Beautiful Land. This points to Antiochus Epiphanes, a ruler from the Syrian division of the Greek empire. He expanded his rule toward Egypt, the East, and the land of Israel.

The little horn grows so proud that it reaches up to the host of heaven. It throws some of the host and some stars down to the earth and tramples them underfoot. In biblical language, God's faithful people and their priests are pictured as a heavenly army and shining stars whom this ruler cruelly persecuted.

This ruler makes himself as great as the Prince of the host, who is God Himself. He stops the daily morning and evening sacrifices and defiles the holy temple in Jerusalem. By attacking the temple worship, he directly defies the Lord.

Because of the sins of God's people, the horn is permitted to overpower the temple service and throw God's truth to the ground. Antiochus burns the sacred scrolls of the law and prospers in his cruel work. God allowed this severe trial as a discipline for their rebellion.

Daniel overhears two holy angels talking with each other. One asks how long this terrible time will last, during which the daily sacrifice is stopped and the sanctuary and the people are trampled down. Even angels care deeply about the suffering of God's people and long to see worship restored.

The answer is given that the affliction will last 2,300 evenings and mornings, after which the sanctuary will be properly cleansed. This refers to the historical restoration of the temple by Judas Maccabaeus after Antiochus defiled it. God sets an exact limit on how long His people must suffer before He brings relief.

differ.view: The 2,300 evenings and mornings are literal natural days, fulfilled in the historical profanation and cleansing of the temple under Antiochus.
Each prophetic day represents a full year, pointing to a long span of 2,300 years before true righteousness covers the earth.
The time was fulfilled literally as days under Antiochus, but because he mirrors the future Antichrist, the days can also foreshadow 2,300 years leading to the end of the world.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: William Miller and later Seventh-day Adventists taught that the 2,300 evenings and mornings were 2,300 years that ended in the autumn of 1844, beginning an investigative judgment in heaven.

notes.meaning: While Daniel tries to understand what he has seen, a figure looking like a man appears before him. A voice calls out across the Ulai canal, commanding the angel Gabriel to explain the vision to Daniel. This commanding voice shows divine authority over the angels, sending Gabriel to guide the prophet.

Gabriel comes close, and Daniel falls facedown in sheer terror before the angel's heavenly brightness. Gabriel addresses him as 'son of man,' reminding him of his human weakness, and explains that the vision concerns the appointed time of the end. The message reveals the final outcome of these worldly kingdoms.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church fathers like Jerome taught that the events under Antiochus serve as a pattern and forerunner for what the final Antichrist will do at the end of history.

notes.meaning: While Gabriel speaks, Daniel collapses into a deep sleep on the ground, overwhelmed by the experience. The angel gently touches him, sets him on his feet, and promises to show him what will happen in the final time of God's wrath against Israel's sins. God strengthens His servants when His word seems too heavy for them to bear.
Gabriel plainly interprets the first symbol: the ram with two horns represents the kings of Media and Persia. This removes any guesswork about the identity of the second great empire.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars view the ram as Media alone rather than a combined Medo-Persian empire, arguing the book of Daniel was written after the events in the second century BC.

notes.meaning: The shaggy goat represents the kingdom of Greece, and its first great horn is its founding king, Alexander the Great. The four horns that replace him are four separate kingdoms that rise from Greece, though none will match his original strength. History perfectly matched this explanation when Alexander's empire split into four weaker realms.

Near the end of those Greek kingdoms, when the sins of the rebels have reached their limit, a fierce and deceitful king will rise to power. This ruler is Antiochus Epiphanes, known for his shameless cruelty and crafty tricks. God permitted his rise only after Israel's unfaithfulness had grown complete.

differ.view: This ruler refers not only to Antiochus of old, but also points directly forward to the Antichrist.
The prophecy strictly describes Antiochus Epiphanes, and applying it directly to the Antichrist stretches the plain meaning of the text.

notes.meaning: This king will wield immense power, though his success will come by deceit and God's permission rather than pure military valor. He will cause shocking destruction, prosper in his schemes, and slaughter mighty leaders as well as God's holy people. Even the worst worldly persecutors act only within the limits God allows.

Using cunning and false promises of peace, he will trick and destroy many people while exalting himself in his own mind. He will even dare to rebel against God Himself, the Prince of princes. Yet he will be destroyed without human hands, struck down suddenly by God through a fatal disease.

Gabriel confirms that the vision of the 2,300 evenings and mornings is completely trustworthy and true. Daniel is told to seal up the vision and guard it, because its events lie hundreds of years in the future. God's promises remain certain even when their fulfillment takes a very long time.

Daniel is left so physically and emotionally drained by the vision of coming suffering that he lies sick for days. When he recovers, he gets up and faithfully returns to his daily duties in the king's court, still astonished by what he had seen. God's people must continue their everyday callings even when carrying heavy burdens.
